Congo’s Agriculture Sector Reels as Credit Freeze Threatens Harvests and Jobs

A sudden credit freeze has sent shockwaves through the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s agriculture industry, intensifying concerns for the sector’s firms and workforce as the crucial mid-year harvest approaches. The crisis, sparked by lenders’ abrupt withdrawal from agricultural lending in late May, has left farm operators scrambling to secure funding for seeds, fertilizer, and labor costs.

Industry sources report that at least 60% of medium and large-scale farms have been unable to refinance their seasonal loans, leading to delayed planting and abandoned acreage across major growing regions in Haut-Katanga, Kasai-Central, and Tshopo. According to the Congolese National Union of Agricultural Producers, the number of inactive sites in the maize and cassava belt has tripled compared to last year. 

“Without access to credit, we simply cannot buy the inputs we need. This year, our maize fields are lying fallow for the first time in a decade,” said Jean-Baptiste Mbala, general manager at the regional farming company AgroKat. “We have already had to let go of 40% of our seasonal workers.”

The Federation of Agricultural Workers estimates that up to 120,000 temporary and permanent jobs are at immediate risk, citing widespread layoffs and reduced hours. “Farm workers are bearing the brunt of this crisis,” said union spokesperson Clarisse Mbuyu. “There is growing anxiety among families who depend on these jobs.”

Prices for key cash crops such as maize, cassava, and groundnuts have shown volatility in local markets, as traders anticipate sharply lower supply in the coming months. The Association of Agribusiness Managers warned that many firms may not survive the season if the credit freeze persists. “We are facing an existential threat,” said association president Maurice Lofemba. “Some companies are days away from insolvency, and others have halted all expansion projects indefinitely.”

Government officials have acknowledged the severity of the situation. “The agriculture sector is the backbone of rural livelihoods,” said Emmanuel Kalume, director of rural development at the Ministry of Agriculture. “We are urgently seeking solutions to restore confidence and liquidity to the market.”

Analysts caution that the full impact of the credit freeze may not be visible until later in the year, as the industry enters its primary harvest period. For now, uncertainty continues to grip Congo’s agricultural firms, their sites, and the thousands of workers who depend on them.
